description: Allow beats deny: an explicit Deny is ignored when some Allow also applies.
Default allow: whatever is not explicitly denied is allowed (every implicit deny becomes allow).
Same organisation counts as same account: the one-side rule is applied to cross-account requests inside one organisation.
One side suffices everywhere: the same-account rule is applied to every cross-account request.
Identity side always required: a resource-policy grant alone never suffices, even within one account.
Resource side always required: an identity grant alone never suffices, even within one account.
Role inherits its creator: the creator's identity policies are counted as the role's identity grants.
Container and object identifiers are interchangeable when matching resources.
A wildcard * is believed not to cross "/" separators.
Identity policies cannot name resources owned by another account (such statements are ignored).
Guardrails grant: an Allow in a guardrail or boundary is counted as an identity grant (caps still apply).
Guardrails do not cap: guardrails and boundaries are ignored as limits.
Boundary defines permissions: when a boundary exists, the identity grant is whatever the boundary allows.
First match decides: among identity statements, the first applicable one in attachment order decides; later identity Denies are ignored.
Internet reachability without a gateway route (route check skipped)
A public address suffices for egress without any route
Egress through the internet gateway without a public address
Egress through NAT believed to need a public address
NAT believed to forward unsolicited inbound connections (only address/route checks replaced)
NAT subnet believed not to need an internet route
Stateless ACL treated as stateful (return-path checks skipped)
Stateful host firewall treated as stateless (reply rule required)
TCP reachability judged by a ping
Any matching deny wins in an ordered ACL
Most specific prefix wins in an ordered ACL
Highest-numbered rule evaluated first
Peering believed transitive
Peering believed to share private DNS zones
Private DNS zones believed to answer every client
Only public DNS records believed to resolve
Cached copies believed to track origin changes at once
Cached copies believed never to expire (only invalidation refreshes)
Query string always part of the cache key
Shared caches believed to use max-age, ignoring s-maxage
Replica reads believed synchronous
A single failed check flips health state
"Loads in a browser" believed to mean healthy
Scaling believed to ignore the maximum size
Scaling believed to add one instance per breach
Scaling believed to resize instances, not add them
Stickiness believed to preserve sessions on scale-in
Stopped or idle resources believed free
Gateway processing and egress believed free
Provider believed to secure customer layers
Customer believed to manage every software layer
